steps.action:
The lantern had burned low by the time Elias Finnley climbed the iron stairs to the gallery of Northhaven Light. Outside, the Atlantic pounded against the black cliffs, sending sheets of salt spray across the stone. The beacon’s beam swept in patient circles—three slow revolutions, a pause, then one bright flash—its coded promise to mariners hidden in the night.

Elias had tended Northhaven for thirty-seven winters. He knew every rivet in the tower, every sigh of the gears, every mood of the sea. Tonight felt different. The wind carried a keener edge, and the gulls had vanished inland hours before dusk. Instinct told him a storm was massing beyond the horizon, stealthy as a prowler.

Down in the engine room, the generator coughed. A weak sputter, then silence.

Elias froze. Without power, the lens would dim and the coast would go dark. He lit his kerosene lamp, set his shoulders, and descended into the tower’s gut. The air smelled of hot oil and ozone. He traced the fault quickly: a cracked fuel line leaking diesel onto the floor. In daylight he could mend it with copper tubing, but now—

A distant thunderclap rolled across the water.

He fetched the emergency patch kit. Hands steady, he cut away the damaged length, spliced the line, tightened clamps until his knuckles ached. When he thumbed the starter, the generator rumbled back to life, a bearish growl that filled him with relief.

Upstairs, the lantern flared brighter, but the gale had arrived. Rain battered the windows like thrown gravel, and the tower swayed just enough to make the antique brass clock on the wall tick an uneven rhythm.

Elias scanned the sea through binoculars. Between waves he glimpsed a fading green light—the running lamp of a trawler straying too near the shoals. He seized the radio microphone. “Northhaven Light to incoming vessel, you’re veering east of the safe channel. Adjust two points starboard.” Static replied. The trawler plowed onward, its hull vanishing behind curtains of rain.

No time for radio. Elias gripped the signal lever and shifted the beacon’s pattern to emergency: quick-quick-long flash. Mariners knew it as the lighthouse keeper’s shout.

A minute passed. Then the trawler’s lamp swung, correcting course. Elias allowed himself a breath. Lightning forked over the sea, illuminating the vessel as it slipped back into safe water.

The storm spent itself toward dawn. Pink light crept over slate clouds, and the sea calmed to a bruised silk. Elias poured coffee from an enamel pot and stepped onto the gallery. Above him, the beacon still turned, steady and sure.

He raised his mug to the horizon. Another night, another quiet victory. No one would note it in the papers, yet somewhere a crew would sail home because a weary man in a stone tower kept faith with a light—and with the endless, watchful sea.
